summary.title: Home Assistant confined — the design of Ch. 5 (§5.14)
summary.description: Figure 5.1 of the capstone report: the design of Chapter 5, drawn on the same canvas as Figure 4.1 so the delta is legible. VISUALISATION ONLY — no threats are enumerated here; they are derived in §4.8 by STRIDE per boundary within an ISO 31000 process (§4.1), and Threat Dragon's own threat generator was not used. All six boundaries now read EXISTS or UNCHANGED; TB2 is UNCHANGED on purpose and carries residual risk R3. Generated by figures/fig_5_1_confined.py; edit that script rather than this file.

text.text:
Compare with Figure 4.1. Five flows drawn there are absent here — F4b (the shared hass.data dict), F5 (reads any integration's stored credentials), F6 (arbitrary file read via hass.config.path),
F8 (direct object access between integrations) and F9 (local network access). None of the five is refused by a check. The config entry store and secrets.yaml are not in the sandbox's
mount namespace, the two integrations are separate processes, and non-public destinations are denied by default, so there is no request to make (§5.6.2, §5.10.2, §5.11.1).

F8 (direct object access between integrations) and F9 (local network access). None of the five is refused by a check. The config entry store and secrets.yaml are not in the sandbox's

text.text:
TB5 and TB6 are crossed by no flow at all, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: in Figure 4.1 those same two locations carried F5, F6, F8, F4b and F9. A boundary nothing crosses is the
strongest form this design produces, because nothing has to decide correctly for it to hold.

text.text:
TB2 is unchanged, and the figure says so rather than quietly upgrading it. The mediator holds a Home Assistant long-lived token, which the platform issues with no read-only and no per-domain
variant, so its credential is exactly as unscoped as the one an integration holds today. That is residual risk R3 (§4.11) — the one boundary of the six this design does not improve.
